question:
Patient note:
A 57-year-old woman is reviewed in the pre-anesthetic bay this morning before a planned laparoscopic right hemicolectomy for a large sessile adenomatous polyp that could not be removed endoscopically; the colorectal team anticipates two to three hours of insufflation-assisted dissection under general endotracheal anesthesia, with three trocars and a small periumbilical extraction site expected. She was admitted five days ago from outpatient clinic so that pulmonary and nutritional status could be optimized after a protracted respiratory illness earlier in the month: three weeks prior she developed pleuritic chest discomfort, low-grade fever, and purulent sputum, saw her primary physician, and a posterior segment right-lower-lobe infiltrate on chest film led to a seven-day course of oral levofloxacin; follow-up imaging obtained on hospital day one now shows only reticular streaking at the base without consolidation, and she has been afebrile since admission, but the episode left her fatigued enough that nursing flow sheets document fewer than two assisted transfers a day, otherwise remaining supine with the head of bed elevated. Blood cultures drawn at presentation remained sterile, and at no point did she meet criteria for sepsis or require vasopressor or intensive care support. Baseline pulmonary history is notable for tobacco-related chronic obstructive lung disease diagnosed a decade ago; she quit smoking after a 35-pack-year exposure but still uses twice-daily inhaled budesonide-formoterol and carries an albuterol rescue inhaler, with the last prednisone-requiring flare eleven months ago. She denies any prior leg clots, sudden chest tightness, or hemoptysis, and no siblings, parents, or children have experienced unexplained thrombosis. She has never been told she has antiphospholipid syndrome, and prior rheumatologic work-up—including anticardiolipin antibody testing—was negative. She has never worn a fiberglass or plaster cast, never sustained fractures of the pelvis, hip, or lower extremities, and the chart contains no record of head trauma, spinal injury, stroke, or polytrauma. The past year has been surgically uneventful; her only operation in adulthood was an uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy sixteen years ago. She has no personal history of cancer, and pathology from previous procedures has never demonstrated malignancy. Cardiovascular review is benign for orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, ankle swelling, or recent admissions for fluid overload, and echocardiography performed last summer for exertional dyspnea showed preserved left ventricular ejection fraction and normal valves. She does not take estrogen preparations, selective estrogen receptor modulators, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or systemic corticosteroids at present; home medications include lisinopril 10 mg daily for hypertension, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, the aforementioned inhalers, and over-the-counter calcium with vitamin D. She does not drink alcohol during the week, enjoys a glass of wine on weekends, and denies illicit drug use. On physical examination this morning she reclines at 30°, converses in full sentences without accessory muscle use, and appears comfortable though somewhat deconditioned. Vital signs: temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 138/74 mm Hg, pulse 80 beats per minute regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96 % on room air. Jugular venous contour is not elevated, the apical impulse is undisplaced, S1 and S2 are crisp without murmurs, rubs, or gallops, and radial and dorsalis pedis pulses are 2+ symmetrically. Pulmonary examination reveals scattered end-expiratory wheezes and faint inspiratory crackles at the right base but otherwise vesicular breath sounds. The abdomen is soft and nondistended; a palpable, mildly tender mass corresponding to the colonic lesion is appreciated in the right lower quadrant, but there is no rebound or guarding. Both lower extremities are warm, well perfused, and show no pitting edema, calf tenderness, or superficial venous engorgement; circumferential measurements taken yesterday by nursing are equal to the millimeter. Skin is intact without pressure injuries despite prolonged recumbency, and passive range of motion is full at the hips, knees, and ankles. Neurologic screening demonstrates intact cranial nerves, 5/5 strength in upper limbs, and preserved sensation throughout; lower-limb strength cannot be fully assessed in bed, but she moves against gravity when encouraged. No intravenous access other than a single 18-gauge peripheral cannula in the left forearm is present; she has never had a tunneled line or implantable port. Laboratory studies drawn at 5 a.m. show hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, hematocrit 37 %, platelet count 228 × 10⁹/L, white blood cells 7.4 × 10⁹/L, sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, creatinine 0.92 mg/dL, AST 22 U/L, ALT 19 U/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, prothrombin time 12.3 s with an international normalized ratio of 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 30 s. Repeat chest radiograph performed yesterday confirms interval improvement of the prior infiltrate, shows mild hyperinflation but no effusion, and verifies a normal cardiac silhouette. Electrocardiogram today reveals normal sinus rhythm at 78 beats/min with nonspecific T-wave flattening in the inferior leads unchanged from previous tracings. Body mass index is 28 kg/m². Airway evaluation demonstrates Mallampati class II, thyromental distance >6 cm, good dentition, and full cervical extension, so anesthesia does not anticipate difficulty with laryngoscopy. She has been nil per os since midnight, bowel prep was completed yesterday afternoon, sequential pneumatic compression sleeves are resting at the bedside awaiting transfer to the operating suite, and no pharmacologic prophylaxis has yet been administered pending completion of operative time-out and line placement.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini surgical VTE risk score sums preoperative risk factors. Using the model with a single lung-disease item:
- Age 41–60 years: age 57 → 1.
- BMI >25 kg/m²: BMI 28 → 1.
- Lung disease: established COPD and pneumonia within the past month satisfy the pulmonary item, counted once → 1.
- Restricted mobility for ≥72 hours: five days largely confined to bed, with only rare assisted transfers → 2.
- Planned major surgery lasting >45 minutes: laparoscopic hemicolectomy expected to take 2–3 hours → 2.
The adenomatous polyp is not malignant, and the peripheral IV is not a central venous catheter. No other qualifying factors are documented.
Total = 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 7.
Final answer: 7
